Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We get asymptotics for the volume of large balls in an arbitrary locally compact group G with polynomial growth. This is done via a study of the geometry of G and a generalization of P. Pansu's thesis. In particular, we show that any such G is weakly commensurable to some simply connected solvable Lie group S, the Lie shadow of G. We also show that large balls in G have an asymptotic shape, i.e. after a suitable renormalization, they converge to a limiting compact set which can be interpreted geometrically. We then discuss the speed of convergence, treat some examples and give an application to ergodic theory. We also answer a question of Burago about left invariant metrics and recover some results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series of nilpotent groups.

This is achieved through a study of the geometry of \(G\) and a generalization of P. Pansu’s thesis. In particular, we show that every such \(G\) is weakly commensurable with a simply connected solvable Lie group \(S\), the Lie shadow of \(G\). Finally, we answer a question of Burago concerning left-invariant metrics and recover some results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series of nilpotent groups.
outputs.L2: We derive asymptotic formulas for the volumes of large metric balls in any locally compact group \(G\) of polynomial growth. The approach relies on analyzing the geometry of \(G\) and extending ideas from P. Pansu’s thesis. A central result is that every such group \(G\) is weakly commensurable with a simply connected solvable Lie group \(S\), called the Lie shadow of \(G\). The work develops a comprehensive asymptotic theory for the volume of large balls in arbitrary locally compact groups of polynomial growth. Its central aim is to understand, with high precision, how the volume of metric balls grows when the radius tends to infinity, and how this growth reflects the large-scale geometry and algebraic structure of the group.

In doing so, it extends the ideas introduced in P. Pansu’s thesis. Pansu studied the asymptotic geometry of nilpotent groups and showed that, after suitable rescaling, large balls converge to limiting shapes related to Carnot–Carathéodory geometry. The present work generalizes this perspective beyond the nilpotent setting, addressing the broader class of locally compact groups with polynomial growth. It analyzes their geometry at large scale and shows that many of the phenomena discovered by Pansu persist in this more general context, although new structural features must be taken into account.

A key structural result is that every locally compact group of polynomial growth is weakly commensurable to a simply connected solvable Lie group, referred to as its Lie shadow. This Lie shadow captures the large-scale geometry of the original group and provides a Lie-theoretic model through which its asymptotic behavior can be studied. In particular, it allows one to reduce many questions about general locally compact groups to questions about solvable Lie groups with controlled algebraic and geometric properties.

The work then proves an asymptotic shape theorem for large balls. After an appropriate renormalization, metric balls in the group converge to a compact limiting set that has a clear geometric interpretation. This limiting shape describes the first-order asymptotic geometry of the group and gives precise information about the leading term in the volume growth of balls. Thus, the volume of large balls is not only shown to have polynomial growth, but its asymptotic behavior is related to an explicit geometric object.

Beyond the main asymptotic results, the work also investigates convergence rates and provides examples illustrating the theory. These examples clarify how the limiting shapes arise and how different algebraic structures influence the asymptotic volume formula. The text further includes an application to ergodic theory, showing how the geometric results can be used in a dynamical context.

Finally, the work discusses several related questions and connections. It addresses a question of Burago concerning left invariant metrics, placing it within the framework of asymptotic shapes and large-scale geometry. It also relates the results to Stoll’s work on growth series of nilpotent groups, explaining how the asymptotic analysis of ball volumes interacts with the more algebraic study of growth functions and their generating series. Overall, the work provides a broad generalization of Pansu’s asymptotic geometry and offers a detailed description of the volume growth and large-scale shape of balls in locally compact groups of polynomial growth.

This work investigates the asymptotic geometry of large balls in arbitrary locally compact groups of polynomial growth. Its main goal is to understand how the volume of such balls behaves at large scales and to describe the limiting geometric objects that arise when the group is viewed from farther and farther away. In doing so, it extends and generalizes Pansu’s foundational results on the asymptotic geometry of finitely generated nilpotent groups to the broader setting of locally compact groups.

A central theme is that, although locally compact groups of polynomial growth may appear quite general, their large-scale geometry is controlled by a much more rigid object. The text shows that every such group is, in an appropriate large-scale sense, weakly commensurable to a simply connected solvable Lie group, called its Lie shadow. This shadow captures the essential asymptotic features of the original group while being more accessible to analysis through Lie-theoretic methods.

Using this reduction, the text studies the behavior of rescaled balls associated with compact generating sets or more general metrics. It proves that, after suitable normalization, these large balls converge to a deterministic limit shape. This limit is described in terms of a graded nilpotent Lie group naturally associated with the original group, equipped with a subFinsler or Carnot–Carathéodory-type metric. As a consequence, one obtains precise asymptotic formulas for volume growth, including the existence of a leading growth constant and a geometric interpretation of that constant as the volume of the limiting unit ball.

The results provide a unified framework for understanding polynomial growth in locally compact groups. They show that the asymptotic volume of balls is not merely governed by the degree of growth, but also by a canonical limit geometry arising from the group’s nilpotent structure. In this way, the work connects large-scale group geometry, Lie theory, and metric geometry.

Beyond the main asymptotic theorems, the text develops several applications. It addresses rates of convergence in volume asymptotics, giving quantitative refinements of the basic limit theorem in certain settings. It also applies the geometric description of large balls to problems in ergodic theory, where Følner sets and averaging sequences play an important role. Since balls in groups of polynomial growth form natural Følner sequences, understanding their asymptotic shape leads to improved control over ergodic averages.

The study further examines invariant metrics on locally compact groups, showing how their large-scale behavior is reflected in the same limiting Carnot-type geometry. This provides a way to compare different metrics and generating sets through their associated limit norms. Finally, the text considers implications for growth series, relating the asymptotic expansion of ball volumes to analytic properties of generating functions that encode growth.

Overall, the work gives a broad and detailed account of the asymptotic geometry of locally compact groups with polynomial growth. By reducing the problem to solvable Lie shadows and proving convergence of rescaled balls to canonical limit shapes, it offers a powerful generalization of Pansu’s theory and supplies tools for applications across geometric group theory, harmonic analysis, ergodic theory, and the study of growth functions.
outputs.L5:
This text explores the connection between Pansu’s work and Lie theory, especially in the study of geometric structures on groups.

Pierre Pansu is well known for his contributions to geometric analysis and metric geometry. One of his important ideas is **Pansu differentiability**, a notion of differentiability adapted to certain non-Euclidean spaces, especially **Carnot groups**. These groups are special examples of **Lie groups**, which are groups that also have the structure of smooth manifolds.

In classical calculus, differentiability is defined using linear maps between Euclidean spaces. However, in many geometric settings, especially those involving sub-Riemannian geometry, the usual derivative is not sufficient. This is where Pansu’s approach becomes important. Pansu differentiability replaces ordinary linear approximation with approximation by group homomorphisms that respect the special dilation structure of Carnot groups.

Lie groups play a central role in this theory because they combine algebra, geometry, and analysis. A Lie group has an associated Lie algebra, which captures its local structure. In Carnot groups, the Lie algebra has a layered structure, allowing one to define natural dilations. These dilations are essential in Pansu’s definition of differentiability.

This connection between Pansu’s ideas and Lie groups has influenced many areas of modern mathematics, including geometric group theory, analysis on metric spaces, and sub-Riemannian geometry. It shows how classical concepts such as derivatives and linear approximation can be extended to more general and highly structured spaces.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematics paper on asymptotic volume growth and limit shapes of balls in locally compact groups of polynomial growth.
counterfactuals.output:
We study the asymptotic geometry of large balls in compactly generated locally compact groups of polynomial growth. For an arbitrary compact symmetric generating set, we prove the existence of a homogeneous limit shape after rescaling the associated word metric, and identify it with the unit ball of a subFinsler metric on the graded nilpotent Lie group arising as the asymptotic cone. As a consequence, the Haar measure of metric balls admits a precise leading-order asymptotic
\[
\mu(B(e,r)) \sim c\, r^d,
\]
where \(d\) is the homogeneous dimension of the nilpotent model and \(c\) is the volume of the limiting unit ball with respect to the induced Haar measure.

The proof combines the structure theory of locally compact groups of polynomial growth with quantitative comparisons between the original group and its nilpotent quotient. We show that compact normal subgroups and finite-index extensions do not affect the limiting geometry, while the large-scale metric is controlled by a Carnot–Carathéodory norm determined by the projection of the generating set to the first layer of the associated graded Lie algebra. In particular, the asymptotic volume constant is expressed intrinsically in terms of this limit norm and the Haar normalization.

These results extend classical limit-shape theorems for finitely generated nilpotent groups to the locally compact setting and provide a unified description of volume growth, asymptotic cones, and metric rescalings for all compactly generated groups of polynomial growth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a research article generalizing Pansu’s thesis to arbitrary locally compact groups with polynomial growth.
counterfactuals.output:
The article extends Pansu’s asymptotic-cone theorem from finitely generated nilpotent groups to **all locally compact, compactly generated groups of polynomial growth**.

Main results:

- **Unique asymptotic cone.**  
  If \(G\) is a locally compact group with polynomial growth and \(\rho\) is a reasonable left-invariant large-scale metric — e.g. a word metric or, more generally, a periodic pseudodistance — then the rescaled spaces
  \[
  (G,\rho/n)
  \]
  converge in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff sense to a canonical limit.

- **Identification of the limit.**  
  The limit is not an arbitrary metric cone: it is a **simply connected graded nilpotent Lie group** equipped with a **subFinsler Carnot–Carathéodory metric**.  
  This generalizes Pansu’s result that finitely generated nilpotent groups have Carnot-group asymptotic cones.

- **Reduction to a nilpotent model.**  
  Although a locally compact group of polynomial growth need not itself be nilpotent or discrete, it has a large-scale nilpotent model. After passing to suitable compact normal subgroups and cocompact subgroups, one obtains a connected nilpotent Lie group, or “nilshadow,” whose associated graded group controls the asymptotic geometry of \(G\).

- **Limit metric from the original metric.**  
  The subFinsler norm on the first layer of the graded Lie algebra is explicitly determined by the large-scale behavior of the original metric \(\rho\). Thus the theorem does not merely identify the topological cone; it also describes the limiting metric.

- **Volume asymptotics.**  
  The paper proves a precise analogue of the Bass–Guivarc’h growth formula. If \(d\) is the homogeneous dimension of the associated graded nilpotent Lie group, then Haar measure satisfies
  \[
  \mu(B_\rho(e,R)) \sim c\,R^d
  \]
  for an explicit constant \(c\) equal to the volume of the unit ball in the limiting Carnot–Carathéodory geometry.

- **Metric-measure convergence.**  
  With appropriately rescaled Haar measure, the balls in \(G\) converge not only as metric spaces but also as measured metric spaces to the unit ball of the limiting Carnot group.

- **Generality beyond word metrics.**  
  The theorem applies to a broad class of “periodic” pseudometrics, including metrics arising from compact generating sets, Riemannian metrics on Lie groups, and other left-invariant large-scale metrics.

In short, the paper shows that every locally compact group of polynomial growth has, at large scale, the same kind of Carnot-group geometry that Pansu discovered for finitely generated nilpotent groups. The asymptotic cone, the growth degree, and the leading volume constant are all governed by a canonical graded nilpotent Lie group associated to \(G\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give a high-level overview of a paper proving volume asymptotics for large balls in locally compact groups of polynomial growth.
counterfactuals.output:
A paper proving **volume asymptotics for large balls in locally compact groups of polynomial growth** typically studies the following problem:

> Let \(G\) be a locally compact compactly generated group with polynomial growth, equipped with a Haar measure and a word-type metric coming from a compact generating set \(S\). How does the volume  
> \[
> \mu(S^n)
> \]
> grow as \(n\to\infty\)?

The main goal is to prove that this volume has a precise polynomial asymptotic.

---

## 1. Background and motivation

For finitely generated groups, polynomial growth means that the size of balls satisfies

\[
|S^n| \leq C n^d
\]

for some constants \(C,d\). Gromov’s theorem says that such groups are virtually nilpotent.

For locally compact groups, one works with a left Haar measure \(\mu\) and compact generating sets \(S\). Polynomial growth means

\[
\mu(S^n) \leq C n^d.
\]

The paper’s aim is not just to show that the growth is polynomial, but to identify the exact leading asymptotic:

\[
\mu(S^n) \sim c\, n^D
\]

for some constant \(c>0\) and some integer or rationally defined exponent \(D\), often called the homogeneous dimension.

---

## 2. Structural reduction

A major part of the proof is structural. Locally compact groups of polynomial growth have a strong algebraic description.

Roughly, after passing to a compact normal subgroup and a finite-index or cocompact subgroup, the group can be related to a connected Lie group of polynomial growth. More precisely, one uses structure theorems showing that such groups are built from:

- compact groups,
- virtually nilpotent discrete groups,
- connected Lie groups of polynomial growth,
- and extensions of these.

The paper reduces the volume asymptotic problem to a more tractable setting, usually a nilpotent or “nilshadow” Lie group.

---

## 3. Nilpotent models and asymptotic cones

The key geometric idea is that a group of polynomial growth looks, at large scale, like a nilpotent graded Lie group.

Given a compact generating set \(S\), one rescales the metric by \(1/n\). The sequence of metric spaces

\[
(G, d_S/n)
\]

converges, in a suitable sense, to a limiting metric space. In the nilpotent case, this limit is a simply connected nilpotent Lie group equipped with a homogeneous metric.

This limiting object is often called the **asymptotic cone** or **Carnot-type model** of the group.

The volume of large balls in \(G\) is then compared to the volume of balls in this limiting graded nilpotent group.

---

## 4. The homogeneous dimension

For a nilpotent Lie group \(N\), the Lie algebra has a descending central series

\[
\mathfrak n = \mathfrak n_1 \supseteq \mathfrak n_2 \supseteq \cdots,
\]

and the associated graded Lie algebra is

\[
\operatorname{gr}(\mathfrak n)
=
\bigoplus_{i\geq 1} \mathfrak n_i/\mathfrak n_{i+1}.
\]

The relevant growth exponent is the **homogeneous dimension**

\[
D = \sum_{i\geq 1} i \cdot \dim(\mathfrak n_i/\mathfrak n_{i+1}).
\]

This is the same exponent appearing in the Bass–Guivarc’h formula for nilpotent groups.

The paper proves that this number governs the leading growth of Haar volume:

\[
\mu(S^n) \sim c(S)\, n^D.
\]

The constant \(c(S)\) depends on the generating set and the normalization of Haar measure, while \(D\) depends only on the large-scale algebraic structure of the group.

---

## 5. The nilpotent case

The proof is clearest for simply connected nilpotent Lie groups.

One chooses coordinates adapted to the lower central series and studies how multiplication behaves under anisotropic dilations. These dilations scale the \(i\)-th layer by \(t^i\). Under rescaling, the original group law converges to the group law of the associated graded nilpotent Lie group.

Large balls in the original group then converge to a unit ball in the graded model. The Haar measure rescales by \(t^D\), so one obtains

\[
\mu(S^n) \sim \operatorname{vol}(B_\infty)\, n^D,
\]

where \(B_\infty\) is the unit ball for the limiting norm or subFinsler metric.

Thus the leading constant is the Haar volume of the limiting unit ball.

---

## 6. Handling non-nilpotent polynomial-growth groups

A locally compact group of polynomial growth need not itself be nilpotent. For example, it may contain compact factors or have a nontrivial semisimple-looking action that is harmless at large scale.

The paper typically deals with this by constructing a **nilshadow**: a nilpotent Lie group that captures the large-scale geometry of the original group.

The nilshadow has the same growth exponent and the same asymptotic cone. Volume growth in the original group is then compared to volume growth in the nilshadow.

This step often uses:

- quotienting by compact normal subgroups,
- passing to cocompact subgroups,
- controlling Haar measure under these operations,
- and proving that these changes affect only bounded multiplicative or additive errors, not the leading asymptotic.

---

## 7. Main theorem

A representative main theorem can be stated informally as follows:

> Let \(G\) be a locally compact compactly generated group of polynomial growth, and let \(S\) be a compact generating set. Then there exist constants \(D\) and \(c(S)>0\) such that
> \[
> \mu(S^n) \sim c(S)n^D.
> \]
> The exponent \(D\) is the homogeneous dimension of the nilpotent graded group associated to \(G\), and \(c(S)\) is the volume of the unit ball in the limiting asymptotic metric.

In many formulations, one also obtains convergence of rescaled balls:

\[
\frac{1}{n} S^n \to B_\infty
\]

in the appropriate geometric sense, with Haar measure convergence.

---

## 8. Significance

The result sharpens the qualitative fact that groups of polynomial growth have polynomially bounded balls. It gives an exact leading term and identifies the geometry responsible for it.

It connects several major themes:

- Gromov’s theorem and virtual nilpotence,
- locally compact group structure theory,
- nilpotent Lie groups and Carnot geometry,
- asymptotic cones,
- Haar measure asymptotics,
- and the Bass–Guivarc’h growth formula.

At a high level, the paper shows that every locally compact group of polynomial growth has a well-defined nilpotent large-scale model, and the volume of large balls in the original group is asymptotically the volume of balls in that model.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a research-paper abstract about polynomial growth groups, weak commensurability to simply connected solvable Lie groups, and asymptotic geometry of large metric balls.
counterfactuals.output:
We study finitely generated groups of polynomial growth through the lens of weak commensurability with simply connected solvable Lie groups and the asymptotic geometry of their large metric balls. Building on the structure theory of Gromov, Guivarc’h, and Pansu, we relate the large-scale geometry of such groups to the associated nilpotent Lie models obtained after passing to finite-index subgroups and compact normal quotients. We show that weak commensurability preserves the asymptotic cone and the leading-order volume geometry of word-metric balls, and that these invariants are governed by the graded nilpotent Lie algebra naturally associated to the lower central series. In particular, large balls, after rescaling, converge in the Gromov–Hausdorff sense to a Carnot–Carathéodory ball in the corresponding simply connected graded nilpotent Lie group.

The paper emphasizes the role of solvable Lie envelopes as continuous models for discrete polynomial-growth groups. Although every finitely generated group of polynomial growth is virtually nilpotent, its realization up to weak commensurability inside a simply connected solvable Lie group provides a flexible framework for comparing word metrics, Haar-volume growth, and asymptotic shapes. We prove that the polynomial degree of growth, the asymptotic volume constant up to normalization, and the sub-Finsler limit geometry are invariant under the relevant commensurability operations. These results clarify how algebraic data—nilpotent rank, central series weights, and the induced norm on the abelianization—determine the coarse and asymptotic geometry of large metric balls. The analysis yields a unified description of polynomial growth groups as discrete approximations to solvable Lie geometries whose asymptotic metric structure is, in fact, nilpotent and Carnot-type.
